conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ll be helping take care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having more weakness in my legs and arms, and it’s been getting worse. I actually fell the other day because my legs gave out, but I only landed on my hands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how long has the weakness been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About a week. It started with shoulder pain, then moved to my legs. My rheumatologist checked my CK and it was high, so she bumped up my steroid dose, but I’m still getting weaker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds like a flare of your polymyositis. We’ve also seen your CK came back at 3578, which is quite elevated. That confirms muscle inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, that’s happened before. But this time it feels worse. I’ve also been more swollen in my legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that too. It’s consistent with your usual flares. We’ll keep you on your diuretic for that. Any chest pain or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m breathing fine. Just the weakness and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also saw your troponin was slightly elevated. But given your history, this can happen during flares and doesn’t necessarily mean heart damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s scary. Is my heart okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think so. Your EKG didn’t show any acute changes, and your heart function has been stable in the past. This is likely due to muscle involvement from the polymyositis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start you on high-dose IV steroids tonight to help calm the flare. Then we’ll transition to oral steroids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your CellCept and your other regular medications. We did increase your warfarin dose because your INR was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been eating more salads—could that affect it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. More vitamin K from greens can lower your INR. We’ll watch it closely and adjust your dose as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CK went up a bit this morning to 3909, but that’s not unusual early in treatment. It should start coming down soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Sometimes it rises before it falls as inflammation starts to respond. We’re still on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I did notice my hands are less swollen today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. The swelling from the fall is improving. We’ll have physical therapy come by to check your strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The rheumatology team reviewed your case. They agree with reducing your IV steroids to 20 mg daily instead of the higher dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s still a strong dose, and safer long-term. You’ll switch to oral steroids soon and your rheumatologist will taper them slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR came back at 4.2 this morning—too high. So we held your warfarin for today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no, is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re being cautious. High INR increases bleeding risk. We’ll restart it tomorrow at a lower dose and monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch for any bruising or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Let us know right away if you see any.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled to get your rituximab infusion today. It’s part of your regular treatment plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I usually get that every few months. Should I expect side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people feel tired or get a mild fever, but we’ll monitor you. Most tolerate it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your CK is coming down to 1829. That means the treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! I do feel a little stronger. I was able to lift my legs a bit in bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Physical therapy agrees you’re improving. They think you’ll be able to go home soon with support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I’ve also been coughing a little—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray showed mild congestion, but no pneumonia. The cough may be from your interstitial lung disease or mild fluid. It’s not severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my blood work—was anything else off?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is low—9.3 on admission, now 10.0. It’s likely from your ongoing vaginal bleeding. We started you on iron pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. My OB/GYN said I have fibroids and will put in an IUD soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that should help stop the bleeding. In the meantime, take the iron daily to rebuild your stores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is back in range at 2.8. We’re going to send you home on a new warfarin schedule: 10 mg and 7.5 mg on alternating days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll write that down. When do I get my next check?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In about a week. We’ll send the order to your clinic. Please make sure they get the result to your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And my steroids—what about those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on 20 mg daily of methylprednisolone. Your rheumatologist will adjust it over time. Don’t stop it suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And CellCept stays the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 1500 mg twice a day. Keep taking it as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go home today with home health support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep an eye on your weight—call if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day. Watch for increased weakness, shortness of breath, or signs of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your rheumatologist soon for your next rituximab dose. Also follow up with OB/GYN for the IUD and get your INR checked next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep up with your meds and therapy. Take care!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we also checked for C. diff because of your antibiotics, but it was negative. No infection there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your heart size is a bit enlarged on X-ray, but stable. We’ll keep managing your CHF with your usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I take my lasix and metoprolol every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s helping keep your heart and lungs stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugars? I know I have diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ve been well-controlled. We restarted your metformin, and you’re doing fine. Keep monitoring at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, the discharge papers are ready. A nurse will go over everything with you before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate all the help.
